analysis.one_liner: Ends the insurance industry's exemption from federal antitrust laws.
analysis.headline: The bill to put insurers under federal antitrust law was referred to three House committees and never got a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would strip the insurance industry's special exemption from federal antitrust law, which since 1945 has let insurers cooperate on rates and share market data without Justice Department or Federal Trade Commission scrutiny. It would let the FTC's competition rules apply to insurance regardless of state regulation, and let the DOJ and FTC jointly publish how they will police joint activity among insurers. It was referred to three committees, sent to two subcommittees, and never received a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who buy health, auto, home, or other insurance, in markets where insurers coordinate on rates or dominate local markets; more competition could mean lower premiums and more choices.

how_it_helps.text: Makes the FTC Act's prohibition of unfair methods of competition apply to the business of insurance even where state law does regulate it [S2][S3].
Repeals the separate McCarran-Ferguson provision (Section 3) that specifically exempts joint rate-making and data-sharing arrangements among insurers from antitrust challenge [S3].
Authorizes the Department of Justice and the Federal Trade Commission to issue joint statements of their antitrust enforcement policies for joint activities in the insurance business [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Insurers, which would face federal antitrust enforcement over coordinated pricing and shared data arrangements they currently conduct under a statutory shield; some compliance and litigation costs could be passed to policyholders.
analysis.who_pays_short: Insurance companies losing their antitrust shield

drawbacks.text: The bill leaves FTC Act rules on matters other than unfair methods of competition applicable to insurance only where state law does not regulate it, so overlapping state and federal enforcement could create compliance uncertainty for insurers [S2][S3].

Removing the Section 3 exemption would expose joint data-pooling arrangements, which even smaller insurers rely on to price policies in states where they lack their own claims data, to antitrust challenge; some such arrangements can legitimately lower costs for consumers [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but indirect: federal antitrust enforcement could break up coordinated pricing in insurance markets where consumers have few alternatives, and the same proposal has resurfaced in later Congresses. The cost is mostly borne by insurers in compliance and litigation, though some could pass through to premiums. A fair criticism is that antitrust enforcement alone does not guarantee more competition in markets where entry is hard, and state regulators argued their oversight already addresses these issues.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Judiciary, Energy and Commerce, and Financial Services committees on the day it was introduced, sent to two subcommittees, and never advanced to a vote before the 111th Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Rep. Peter DeFazio introduced the Insurance Industry Competition Act of 2009 on March 18, 2009, with five original cosponsors [S1][S3].
The same day, it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and, in addition, to the Energy and Commerce and Financial Services committees [S1][S5].

In the following weeks it was referred to the Energy and Commerce subcommittee on Commerce, Trade and Consumer Protection (March 19, 2009) and the Judiciary subcommittee on Courts and Competition Policy (April 27, 2009); no further action was recorded [S5].
The bill ended the Congress with 12 cosponsors, 11 Democrats and 1 Republican, having never received a hearing vote, a committee vote, or a floor vote [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The insurance industry is better off: it kept the federal antitrust exemption it has held since the McCarran-Ferguson Act of 1945, and no chamber ever considered taking it away.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers, who kept their antitrust exemption

against.name: Insurance industry

against.what_they_did: During the 2009-2010 health care debate, the industry and its trade associations publicly defended the state-regulation framework and opposed proposals to strip the federal antitrust exemption for insurers.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never got a vote, so no roll call exists; its 12 cosponsors split 11 Democrats and 1 Republican, suggesting a Democratic-leaning but not strictly partisan appeal.

industries.note: The bill removes the industry's 1945-era exemption from federal antitrust law, exposing coordinated rate-setting and data-sharing to DOJ and FTC enforcement. Consumers in concentrated insurance markets could see more competition and lower prices, so the industry's interest in keeping the exemption runs against theirs.

The bill preserves state regulation for FTC Act matters outside unfair competition but inserts federal antitrust enforcement on top of it, which state regulators have historically resisted as duplicative. For consumers, federal enforcement adds a backstop where state oversight falls short.
